books.section: Topic 7.5 World War I: Military and Diplomacy
United States and World War I (1914-1921)
The Progressive Era and World War I (1900-1920)

primary_sources: Woodrow Wilson, War Message to Congress, April 2, 1917
Woodrow Wilson, Fourteen Points address, January 8, 1918
Henry Cabot Lodge, Senate speech, August 12, 1919

source: original; documents drawn from public-domain sources and book-grounded paraphrases
prompt: Evaluate the extent to which the United States' entry into World War I and its role in the peace settlement changed the nation's position in the world from 1914 to 1920.

documents.title: Wilson asks for war
documents.source: President Woodrow Wilson, War Message to Congress, April 2, 1917. Verbatim excerpt, public domain.
documents.text: "The world must be made safe for democracy. Its peace must be planted upon the tested foundations of political liberty. We have no selfish ends to serve. We desire no conquest, no dominion. We seek no indemnities for ourselves, no material compensation for the sacrifices we shall freely make."
documents.sourcing: Wilson, the president, stating his war aims to Congress. A public case for war, meant to rally a reluctant country behind an idealistic cause.

documents.title: The Zimmermann telegram
documents.source: German Foreign Secretary Arthur Zimmermann to the German minister in Mexico, January 16, 1917. Decoded text, verbatim excerpt, public domain.
documents.text: "We intend to begin on the first of February unrestricted submarine warfare. We shall endeavor in spite of this to keep the United States of America neutral. In the event of this not succeeding, we make Mexico a proposal of alliance on the following basis: make war together, make peace together, generous financial support and an understanding on our part that Mexico is to reconquer the lost territory in Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona."
documents.sourcing: Zimmermann, the German foreign secretary, writing in secret code to his minister in Mexico. A private instruction, never meant for American eyes, that British intelligence intercepted and decoded.

documents.title: The Fourteen Points
documents.source: President Woodrow Wilson, Fourteen Points address to Congress, January 8, 1918. Verbatim excerpts, public domain.
documents.text:
"I. Open covenants of peace, openly arrived at, after which there shall be no private international understandings of any kind but diplomacy shall proceed always frankly and in the public view."

"XIV. A general association of nations must be formed under specific covenants for the purpose of affording mutual guarantees of political independence and territorial integrity to great and small states alike."
documents.sourcing: Wilson, the president, laying out American war aims nine months after the U.S. declaration of war. A public program meant to win support at home and abroad for a new kind of peace.

documents.title: I Want You for U.S. Army
documents.source: James Montgomery Flagg, recruiting poster, 1917. Public domain; Library of Congress LCCN93509735.
documents.sourcing: Flagg, an artist working for the Army's recruiting drive, picturing Uncle Sam pointing at the viewer. A poster meant to turn viewers into soldiers after the declaration of war.

documents.title: Article 231 of the Treaty of Versailles
documents.source: Treaty of Versailles, Article 231, signed June 28, 1919. Verbatim, public domain.
documents.text: "The Allied and Associated Governments affirm and Germany accepts the responsibility of Germany and her allies for causing all the loss and damage to which the Allied and Associated Governments and their nationals have been subjected as a consequence of the war imposed upon them by the aggression of Germany and her allies."
documents.sourcing: The treaty itself, in its reparations section. The clause that made Germany accept blame for the war, written by the victors and presented to German delegates to sign.

documents.title: Lodge against the League
documents.source: Senator Henry Cabot Lodge, speech in the Senate on the League of Nations, August 12, 1919. Verbatim excerpt, public domain.
documents.text: "You may call me selfish if you will, conservative or reactionary, or use any other harsh adjective you see fit to apply, but an American I was born and an American I have remained all my life. I can never be anything else but an American, and I must think of the United States first, and when I think of the United States first in an arrangement like this, I am thinking of what is best for the world."
documents.sourcing: Lodge, chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, speaking against the League. A senator defending American sovereignty against a treaty he believed would bind the nation's hands.

documents.title: The Child Who Wanted to Play by Himself
documents.sourcing: Punch, a British magazine, drawing Wilson leading a small child marked U.S.A. toward the Temple of Peace. A British view of American refusal, published days after the Senate rejected the treaty.

rubric.criterion: Thesis: earns the point for a historically defensible claim that answers the prompt, stating the extent to which entry into World War I and the peace settlement changed the nation's position in the world from 1914 to 1920, with a clear line of reasoning.
rubric.notEarned: Restating the prompt with no claim about the extent of change does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Contextualization: earns the point for describing a broader historical context relevant to the prompt, such as American neutrality and trade with the Allies, the Progressive era's faith in government, or the long tradition of avoiding European entanglements.
rubric.notEarned: A sentence of background with no link to the argument, or background from a later century, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (first point): earns the point for describing specific and relevant evidence from at least three documents to support an argument about the changing American position in the world.
rubric.notEarned: Naming documents without describing their content does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (second point): earns the point for using the content of at least six documents to support an argument about the changing American position in the world.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than six documents, or describing them without tying them to the argument, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence beyond the documents: earns the point for describing a specific and relevant example beyond the documents, such as the Selective Service Act, the convoys that broke the submarine campaign, the Meuse-Argonne Offensive, or the Senate's November 1919 votes.
rubric.notEarned: A vague reference to the war with no specific example does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Sourcing: earns the point for explaining the relevance of a document's author, purpose, audience, or historical situation, such as Wilson stating war aims to Congress, Zimmermann writing in secret code, or Punch drawing a British view of American refusal.
rubric.notEarned: Naming an author without explaining why the authorship matters does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Complexity: earns the point for demonstrating a complex understanding, such as qualifying the extent of change by area, explaining that American power grew while American commitments did not, or weighing the new global role against the refusal of the League.
rubric.notEarned: A second example with no qualification or weighing does not earn the point.

modelOutline:
Thesis: Entering World War I changed the United States from a neutral trading nation into a world power, but the peace settlement changed its position only partway: America gained military and economic weight while refusing the binding commitment that would have made it a leader of the new order.
Context: The United States entered the war after three years of neutrality, trading heavily with the Allies while German submarines attacked its shipping, and in the Progressive era the federal government had already grown used to directing the economy.
Evidence: Documents 1-3 show the idealistic case for war and peace: Wilson's call to make the world safe for democracy, the Zimmermann telegram that turned opinion toward war, and the Fourteen Points promising open diplomacy and a league of nations. Documents 4-7 show the limits: the Flagg poster raising an army, Article 231 imposing a punitive peace, Lodge defending American sovereignty, and the Punch cartoon showing the United States refusing the League.
Beyond the documents: The Selective Service Act raised an army of four million, American troops helped stop the German offensives of 1918 and fought the Meuse-Argonne Offensive, and the Senate rejected the treaty in November 1919 and again in March 1920.
Sourcing: Wilson states public war aims to Congress, Zimmermann writes in secret code never meant for American eyes, and Punch draws the American refusal from a British point of view.
Complexity: The change split by area. American military and economic power grew decisively, while American diplomacy stayed guarded: the country would lead disarmament talks and trade in the 1920s but would not join the League it had designed.
